triage.name: Orbital cellulitis
triage.reason: Serious orbital infection with proptosis, pain with eye movement and vision change; high-stakes emergency case distinguished from preseptal cellulitis by exam and imaging.

demographics: More common in children, especially under 10 years
Also occurs in older adults, often after sinusitis or dental infection

risk_factors.text: Dental infection or recent dental procedure
Recent eye surgery or orbital injection

exposures: Recent upper respiratory infection in the household or community

chief_complaints.text: My eye is swollen and bulging out
My eye hurts and it hurts to move it
My eye is red and swollen shut
I have a fever and feel awful

hpi.onset: Subacute, developing over hours to a few days
hpi.progression: Starts as eyelid swelling and redness, then progresses to proptosis, pain with eye movement, and blurred or double vision; may worsen rapidly over hours
hpi.location: One eye and the surrounding orbit, sometimes with adjacent sinus or facial pain
hpi.radiation: Pain may radiate to the forehead or cheek
hpi.quality: Deep, aching, pressure-like pain; sharp with eye movement
aggravating: Pressing on the eye or eyelid

associated_symptoms.text: Facial pain or pressure over the sinuses

pertinent_negatives: No history of recent eye surgery or trauma
No prior episodes of similar eye swelling
No skin infection around the eye

argues_against: Isolated otitis media without orbital signs

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may not report vision changes or pain with eye movement; they present with eyelid swelling, fever, irritability, and refusal to open the eye.
May have less fever and less pain despite severe infection; proptosis may be less obvious due to age-related tissue changes.
Can progress rapidly with minimal inflammatory signs; fever may be absent and fungal pathogens are more likely.
Higher risk of fungal orbital infection (mucormycosis) with rapid progression, black necrotic eschars, and severe headache.

general.mild: Alert, uncomfortable, eyelid swelling and redness on one side, no systemic toxicity
general.moderate: Ill-appearing, febrile, proptotic eye with pain on movement, prefers to keep the eye closed
general.severe: Toxic-appearing, febrile, marked proptosis with chemosis and limited eye movement, distressed by pain
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, lethargic or confused, severe proptosis with vision loss, may have cranial nerve deficits

Inspect the eyes from above and below, or use a Hertel exophthalmometer

Test extraocular movements in all directions

Ask about double vision, or test with red glass/cover test

Measure intraocular pressure with a tonometer if safe

findings.finding: Cranial nerve deficit (e.g., impaired extraocular movement or facial sensation)

findings.maneuver: Assess neck stiffness and Kernig/Brudzinski signs if meningitis is a concern
Inspect the oral cavity and dentition
findings.finding: No dental abscess or oral lesions

imaging.study: CT orbits and sinuses with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Adults and older children; the study of choice to distinguish orbital from preseptal cellulitis and to find an abscess

Proptosis with anterior displacement of the globe
Subperiosteal or orbital abscess (rim-enhancing fluid collection)
Opacification of the adjacent ethmoid or maxillary sinuses
Preseptal soft tissue swelling anterior to the orbital septum
Intracranial extension or cavernous sinus thrombosis

imaging.study: MRI orbits and brain with and without IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected intracranial extension, cavernous sinus thrombosis, or when CT is nondiagnostic

findings.text: Orbital fat and muscle inflammation with contrast enhancement
Subperiosteal or orbital abscess with rim enhancement
Cavernous sinus thrombosis (filling defect or nonenhancing sinus)

imaging.preferred_when: Not the study of choice; may be done first when intracranial pathology is the main concern

imaging.preferred_when: Rarely used; limited by eyelid swelling and operator dependence

findings.text: Thickened orbital tissues or fluid collection may be seen

imaging.study: Plain radiograph of the orbits or sinuses

findings.text: Usually nonspecific; may show sinus opacification but cannot distinguish preseptal from orbital cellulitis

Supports bacterial infection and provides a baseline to follow

initial.test: CT orbits and sinuses with IV contrast
initial.why: Distinguishes orbital from preseptal cellulitis and identifies an abscess or sinus source

supporting.why: Adds to the inflammatory picture and helps track response
Identifies diabetes, a risk factor for mucormycosis

supporting.only_if: the patient is hypotensive, tachycardic, or toxic-appearing

supporting.test: MRI orbits and brain with and without IV contrast
supporting.why: Better defines intracranial extension or cavernous sinus thrombosis
supporting.only_if: intracranial extension or cavernous sinus thrombosis is suspected, or CT is nondiagnostic

not_indicated.test: Plain radiograph of the orbits or sinuses
not_indicated.why: Cannot distinguish preseptal from orbital cellulitis and does not change management
Limited by eyelid swelling and less accurate than CT
No role in the evaluation of orbital infection
Not needed unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis
Not routinely helpful in orbital cellulitis

not_indicated.test: MRI orbits and brain with and without IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Reserved for suspected intracranial extension or nondiagnostic CT
not_indicated.only_if: intracranial extension or cavernous sinus thrombosis is suspected, or CT is nondiagnostic

decision_points: Pregnancy test before CT in anyone who could be pregnant
Distinguish preseptal from orbital cellulitis by proptosis, pain with eye movement, and limited eye movement; CT confirms orbital involvement
Urgent ophthalmology and ENT consultation when proptosis, vision change, or an abscess is present
Surgical drainage is considered for a subperiosteal or orbital abscess, especially with vision loss or failure to improve on antibiotics
Blood cultures and sinus cultures are obtained when systemic infection or a surgical source is suspected

differential.name: Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis
differential.why_considered: The most common and most important look-alike: infection limited to the tissues anterior to the orbital septum, with eyelid swelling and redness that can look identical at first glance.
differential.trigger: Eyelid swelling and redness without proptosis, pain with eye movement, or vision change

history: Eyelid swelling and redness without bulging of the eye
No double vision
No change in vision
Often follows a skin break, insect bite, or stye
exam: Normal visual acuity and normal pupils
labs: White count may be normal or only mildly elevated
imaging: CT shows soft tissue swelling anterior to the orbital septum only, with normal orbital fat and muscles

differential.name: Cavernous sinus thrombosis
differential.why_considered: A thrombotic complication of the same sinonasal and facial infections that cause orbital cellulitis, and it can present with proptosis, eyelid swelling, and cranial nerve deficits.
differential.trigger: Bilateral eye findings, severe headache, or cranial nerve deficits in a patient with orbital infection

history: Severe headache, often the earliest and worst symptom
Rapid progression over hours
Fever and rigors
exam: Bilateral proptosis and eyelid swelling (spread across the sinuses)
Cranial nerve deficits, especially III, IV, V1/V2, and VI
imaging: MRI with contrast shows a filling defect or nonenhancing cavernous sinus
CT venography shows absent flow in the cavernous sinus

differential.name: Orbital inflammatory disease (idiopathic orbital pseudotumor)
differential.why_considered: Noninfectious inflammation of the orbit that causes painful proptosis, eyelid swelling, and limited eye movement, mimicking infection.

history: Subacute onset over days to weeks rather than hours
Often no fever or systemic illness
May be recurrent
May be associated with autoimmune disease
exam: Proptosis and painful eye movement but no purulent discharge
labs: Inflammatory markers may be normal or mildly elevated
Thyroid function and thyroid antibodies may be abnormal if thyroid eye disease
imaging: CT or MRI shows diffuse orbital fat and muscle inflammation without an abscess or sinus opacification
May involve the lacrimal gland or extraocular muscles in a pattern atypical for infection

differential.name: Thyroid eye disease (Graves ophthalmopathy)
differential.why_considered: Causes proptosis, eyelid swelling, and diplopia, and can be mistaken for orbital infection when inflammation is active.

history: Gradual onset over weeks to months
History of hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism, or prior thyroid disease
No fever or acute pain
Smoking history is common
exam: Restrictive strabismus with diplopia on upgaze
No pain with eye movement or only mild discomfort
labs: Abnormal TSH, free T4, or thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin
imaging: CT or MRI shows enlarged extraocular muscle bellies with sparing of the tendons

differential.name: Orbital tumor (e.g., rhabdomyosarcoma in children, lymphoma or metastasis in adults)
differential.why_considered: A mass in the orbit can cause proptosis, eyelid swelling, and vision change, and may be mistaken for infection when it presents subacutely.
differential.trigger: Proptosis that progresses over weeks without fever or sinus symptoms, especially in a child

history: Gradual onset over weeks to months
No fever, no recent sinusitis or skin infection
Weight loss, night sweats, or known malignancy in adults
exam: Proptosis that is painless or only mildly painful
Palpable mass or resistance in the orbit
No purulent discharge or sinus tenderness
May have ptosis or a fixed globe
labs: Normal white count and inflammatory markers
Lactate dehydrogenase may be elevated in lymphoma
imaging: CT or MRI shows a discrete soft tissue mass, bone destruction, or remodeling
No rim-enhancing abscess or sinus opacification

differential.name: Mucormycosis (rhinocerebral or orbital)
differential.why_considered: An angioinvasive fungal infection that can spread from the sinuses into the orbit and cause proptosis, vision loss, and cranial nerve deficits, especially in diabetes or immunosuppression.
differential.trigger: Diabetic or immunocompromised patient with sinusitis, orbital swelling, black necrotic eschars, and rapidly worsening vision

history: Poorly controlled diabetes, especially with ketoacidosis
Immunosuppression, transplant, or prolonged corticosteroid use
Rapid progression over hours to days
Severe headache and facial pain
exam: Black necrotic eschar on the nasal mucosa or palate
Facial numbness or cranial nerve deficits
Vision loss out of proportion to external findings
labs: Fungal hyphae on biopsy or culture
imaging: CT or MRI shows sinus opacification with orbital and intracranial extension
Absence of normal sinus enhancement or bone destruction

differential.name: Allergic conjunctivitis with periorbital swelling
differential.why_considered: Causes red, swollen, watery eyes and eyelid puffiness that can be mistaken for early periorbital infection.

history: Itching is the dominant symptom
Bilateral involvement
Seasonal or exposure-related pattern
No fever or pain

differential.name: Traumatic orbital hematoma
differential.why_considered: Trauma can cause proptosis, eyelid swelling, and limited eye movement from a hematoma or fracture, resembling infection.

history: Recent trauma to the eye or face
Sudden onset after injury
No fever or systemic illness
exam: Possible step-off or crepitus from orbital fracture
labs: Normal white count and inflammatory markers
imaging: CT shows hematoma, orbital fracture, or air in the orbit

severity.mild: Early orbital cellulitis: eyelid swelling and mild proptosis, pain with eye movement, no vision change, low-grade or no fever, normal visual acuity
severity.moderate: Established orbital cellulitis: clear proptosis, chemosis, limited eye movement, fever, leukocytosis, but vision preserved
severity.severe: Orbital cellulitis with a subperiosteal or orbital abscess, or with vision loss, afferent pupillary defect, or cranial nerve deficits
severity.critical: Orbital cellulitis with intracranial extension, cavernous sinus thrombosis, or sepsis with hemodynamic instability

red_flags.finding: Decreased visual acuity or color vision
red_flags.meaning: Optic nerve or retinal compromise; needs urgent imaging and ophthalmology evaluation

red_flags.finding: Severe proptosis with a fixed, immobile globe
red_flags.meaning: Orbital compartment syndrome or large abscess; may need urgent surgical decompression

red_flags.finding: Cranial nerve deficits or altered mental status
red_flags.meaning: Intracranial extension or cavernous sinus thrombosis
Cavernous sinus thrombosis until proven otherwise
Sepsis; needs resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics

red_flags.finding: Black necrotic eschar on nasal mucosa or palate in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient
red_flags.meaning: Mucormycosis; needs urgent biopsy and antifungal therapy

complications.name: Subperiosteal abscess
clues: CT showing a rim-enhancing fluid collection along the orbital wall

complications.name: Orbital abscess
clues: CT or MRI showing an intraorbital rim-enhancing collection

complications.name: Vision loss from optic neuropathy or retinal ischemia
clues: Severe proptosis with increased intraocular pressure

complications.name: Cavernous sinus thrombosis
clues: MRI or CT venography showing a filling defect

complications.name: Intracranial extension (meningitis, epidural or brain abscess)
clues: MRI showing meningeal enhancement or intracranial collection

complications.name: Optic atrophy and permanent visual impairment
clues: Persistent vision loss after resolution of infection

special_populations.differences: Most common in children under 10; young children may not report pain with eye movement or vision change, presenting instead with eyelid swelling, fever, irritability, and refusal to open the eye. Sinusitis is the usual source. CT is used when orbital involvement is suspected, and younger children may need sedation for imaging.
May have less fever and less pain despite severe infection; proptosis may be less obvious. Dental and sinus sources are common. Higher risk of atypical organisms and complications.
Can progress rapidly with minimal inflammatory signs; fever may be absent. Fungal pathogens, especially Mucorales, are more likely and require urgent biopsy and antifungal therapy.
Higher risk of fungal orbital infection (mucormycosis) with rapid progression, black necrotic eschars, severe headache, and vision loss. Glucose control is part of management.
Imaging should avoid ionizing radiation when possible; MRI without gadolinium or with gadolinium after weighing benefits is preferred. Antibiotic choices must consider fetal safety.

key_questions.question: When did the eye swelling start, and how fast has it gotten worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset over hours to a few days with rapid progression; a slow course over weeks suggests a noninfectious or neoplastic cause

key_questions.question: Does the eye look like it is bulging out, or is it just the eyelid that is swollen?
key_questions.looking_for: Proptosis (globe pushed forward) points to orbital rather than preseptal involvement

key_questions.question: Does it hurt when you move your eye?
key_questions.looking_for: Pain with eye movement, a hallmark of orbital involvement

key_questions.question: Has your vision changed — blurry, dimmer, double, or loss of color?
key_questions.looking_for: Blurred or decreased vision, diplopia, or color change; vision loss is a sight-threatening red flag

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever, chills, or felt generally unwell?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever and systemic illness supporting infection

key_questions.question: Have you had a recent cold, sinus infection, or facial pain and pressure?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent or current sinusitis or upper respiratory infection, the most common source

key_questions.question: Any recent tooth pain, dental work, or dental infection?
Any recent injury to the eye or face, or eye surgery or injection?
key_questions.looking_for: Trauma or recent ocular procedure as a portal of entry

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, or any condition or medicine that weakens your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetes or immunosuppression, which raises concern for fungal infection such as mucormycosis

key_questions.question: Are you taking steroids or other immunosuppressive medicines?
key_questions.looking_for: Corticosteroids, transplant drugs, or biologics that increase risk of severe or fungal infection

key_questions.question: Any headache, neck stiffness, confusion, or weakness?
key_questions.looking_for: Intracranial extension, meningitis, or cavernous sinus thrombosis

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy status before CT imaging and to guide antibiotic choice

reasoning_points: Unilateral eyelid swelling and redness with proptosis, pain with eye movement, and often fever
Recent or current sinusitis, upper respiratory infection, or dental infection as the usual source
Distinguishing orbital from preseptal cellulitis by proptosis, pain with eye movement, limited eye movement, and vision change
Reduced visual acuity, afferent pupillary defect, or cranial nerve deficits indicating a sight- or life-threatening complication
Leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance and elevated inflammatory markers supporting bacterial infection
Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits and sinuses showing orbital fat stranding, muscle enlargement, sinus opacification, or an abscess
Considering fungal infection (mucormycosis) in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient with rapid progression or necrotic eschar
Urgent ophthalmology and ENT involvement, with surgical drainage considered for an abscess or vision loss

easy: Child with recent sinusitis and a swollen, bulging red eye
Clear proptosis with pain on eye movement and fever
Leukocytosis and sinus opacification on CT
Classic distinction from preseptal cellulitis is straightforward
medium: Early orbital cellulitis with eyelid swelling and only mild proptosis, hard to separate from preseptal cellulitis
Older adult with little fever or pain despite significant infection
Mild pyuria or nonspecific symptoms suggesting another cause
Patient with dental source rather than obvious sinusitis
hard: Diabetic or immunocompromised patient with rapidly progressive disease and concern for mucormycosis
Young child who cannot report pain with eye movement or vision change, presenting with irritability and refusal to open the eye
Bilateral findings suggesting cavernous sinus thrombosis
Proptosis that progresses over weeks without fever, raising concern for an orbital tumor
Vision loss or cranial nerve deficits at presentation indicating intracranial extension
